description: §17.1.2 + §17.1.2.1 — `if=` on an `<engine>` gates its RENDERED OUTPUT and nothing else. `@shown` seeds false and nothing flips it, so neither variant arm may exist in the DOM: before this widening the attribute generated ZERO code, so the `initial=` arm rendered unconditionally and stayed visible PERMANENTLY on a clean exit-0 compile. The discriminating half is what happens WHILE the gate is false: clicking #to-on takes a real Off -> On transition, so the auto-declared engine cell must read On (§51.0.C — the declaration is not gated) and <onTransition to=.On> must have fired exactly once (§51.0.H — lifecycle is not gated), while #arm-off and #arm-on both stay at count 0. An implementation that gated the engine's LIFECYCLE instead of its RENDER passes the two count-0 assertions and fails both state assertions.
rationale: §17.1.2 admits `if=` on `<engine>` and scopes §17.1 semantics to "the engine's mount subtree (the rendered arm)". §17.1 fixes what that means: "When `expr` evaluates to false, the element is NOT rendered. It does not exist in the DOM." §17.1.2.1 then fixes what it does NOT mean: the auto-declared engine variable (§51.0.C) "is declared and readable REGARDLESS of `expr`", and `rule=` enforcement, `effect=`, `<onTransition>`, `<onTimeout>` and `<onIdle>` "remain LIVE while `expr` is false — transitions continue to occur, only their rendering is withheld". The stated reason is that tying an engine's lifecycle to a render predicate would make `if=` state-destroying and break the §51.0.A singleton invariant, since a cross-file `<EngineName/>` mount (§51.0.D) would observe a different engine depending on an unrelated page's conditional.
